who-this-is-for.text: Naming is an instance of the registry, not a second model: the same seven edges, the same tokens, the same refusals, with naming's own rule about who may certify what. Open the simulator and switch the profile picker to the naming profile.

what-you-can-do.text: Watch the journey. The controller books alice with one insertActive, certified by the controller's signature, and the active token goes to the record. A quorum then retires it with one updateTerminal: the active token is burned and the leaf can never move again. The control key alone cannot do this — the rule is the committed recovery key revealed and signing, or a distinct-member quorum, and the control key on its own is neither.

Then a folded read mints the Over witness, which needs no approval at all: anyone may attest a retired name. Then another, because the terminal witness is plural — the attestation is a read, so both copies are true. Burn them both and the leaf is still terminal. An attestation says something that stays true whether or not you keep the token.

Below the journey, twenty-four naming rows across six sections are replayed in your browser, each a verdict the Lean computed. Below that, twenty-one lifecycle rows: seeding the consumer with its pinned policies, moving a payment destination while the registry root stays put, revealing the committed recovery key, and both retirement routes with the refusals that guard them.

what-you-see-when-it-is-refused.text: Every refusal names its own condition; a generic exception is a defect. Booking a name that is already booked is already-booked. Moving a retired name, by any edge at all, is terminal-immutable. Attesting a name that is not retired names the state it found instead.

Two rows are deliberately different names. Naming defines no delete, so a delete through the naming profile is naming-no-delete. A retirement that met neither authorization route is a different failure — naming-retirement-uncertified — and must not wear delete's name. The two approval rows are the ones worth trying by hand: an approval under the right policy for a different request is refused, and so is no approval at all on any edge but the read.

how-the-pieces-relate.text: Naming does not re-implement the registry and the page does not re-implement naming. The previous simulator did re-implement it, in about nine hundred lines of JavaScript, and when the Lean moved those lines went on describing a model that no longer existed while still reporting green. What the page transcribes is the replay: every row is a verdict the Lean computed, and the page recomputes or re-checks it in front of you.

what-is-proved-and-what-is-checked-here.text: The naming instance carries seven theorem declarations, its lifecycle six and its wire encoding five — eighteen in all, each proved in Lean from the standard axioms alone and each in its own manifest with its own compiled gate, separate from the registry's twenty-four.

The naming statements are stated as characterisations rather than one-way implications: the retirement rule says exactly when retirement is certified, so a model that certified more than the rule allows fails them as surely as one that certified less. Finite checks are finite: the replays measure the transcription on its rows; they do not prove the quantified statements, and they do not make the candidate accepted.

fixture-fields-and-finite-model-limits.text: The playable claim card carries four fixture fields: an optional canonical payment destination, a canonical controller address, a thirty-two-byte next-control commitment, and a threshold quorum. The pending request also stores its refund address inside the Insert commitment, and cancellation can only copy it. No fee, deposit, price, bond, or refund-value schedule is invented. Retirement request withdrawal remains a distinct refusal case.

status-of-this-candidate.text: The claim, fold, and resolve naming profile is an unaccepted candidate: proven in Lean, replayed in the simulator, and playable in the browser. The Nix-built documentation archive packages its raw model, corpus, replay inputs, and exact identities for review. Building that bundle is not release publication or on-chain acceptance. The live preview is bound to the pull-request head and states that the candidate is unaccepted.

finding-alice.text: The asset name is the registry key. The historical Koios query shows how to find the live witness under each policy, but it is not the read path for the dated preprod demos. Those require an indexed chain point and freshness. The holding address and inline datum identify the live record or completion custody. The token at that output is the witness read; this example does not query the root or walk history.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: A name is one key in the registry's authenticated map, and the value of that key is a single byte: zero for absent, one for active, two for terminal. Seven requests move a key and nothing else does, and each one moves a witness token — the thing a reader actually looks at, never the root. The witnesses obey four laws. A witness moves only inside a fold. The fold decides how many and where, summing the witness column of the requests it consumed so the transaction's mint must equal that sum exactly. A terminal witness is its holder's to destroy, because saying a name is over costs the registry nothing. And the asset name is the registry key, so identity is the pair of policy and key. No application script runs at fold time: naming certifies an edge in advance by minting one approval whose name binds the edge, the key, the owner and the destination, and the cage recomputes that name from the request itself.
